why: A fall-to-winter ice and snow route in the Snowy Range, which holds no glacier; the ice season is the snow season.
A short snow couloir in the Snowy Range with no glacier, and the listing says axe and crampons help to reach it until July.
Fall and early-winter ice and mixed line in the Snowy Range with snow and turf above; no glacier exists there, and the usual season is snowy.
The route starts by climbing a snowfield below a buttress in a cirque with no glacier, so the snow is a plain snowfield, not crevassed ice.
The standard way in is the snowy Valhalla Traverse, but the Teton Glacier is a listed alternative, and the face holds snow and ice into summer.
Guides describe the Teton Glacier approach with crevasses and a moat, but the Valhalla and Cascade approaches avoid it, so the normal line is not settled.
It begins atop the Grandstand, reached by the snowy Valhalla Traverse or by the Teton Glacier, and its own text lists easy snow on the route.
The stored text names a Colchuck Glacier approach that looks misfiled from a Washington route, and I found nothing online about this Kagevah line; the couloir is steep snow and ice.
A snowfield and narrow couloir on a peak at the head of Paintbrush Canyon with no glacier, climbed with axe and crampons and descended on moderate snow.
The couloir is a steep snow gully without a glacier, with trip reports showing snow and crampons into June and a steep snow stretch even late.
A rock buttress reached by trail from Lonesome Lake, with an ice axe needed only in early season.
The approach is the Garnet Canyon south fork talus to the col with no glacier, but the rack notes an axe for approach and descent, so lingering snow is not settled.
The line crosses the crevassed Sphinx Glacier and then climbs a snow couloir on crampons that holds snow until July.
A rock face reached by trail and talus in a canyon without glaciers, but the snow cone below the couloir is used as a landmark and may be crossed.
Sources show a snow couloir with crampons and an ice tool, shared with the Triple Glaciers route at the top, and none says whether a glacier is crossed.
The text describes a rock buttress and a descent by talus to a snowfield and lake with no glacier mentioned, but the snowfield's state in season is not clear.
It is a walk-up couloir separate from the Middle Teton Glacier line, but reports range from melted out to snow all the way, so snow depends on the year.
The start col is reached across the Dinwoody Glacier with a bergschrund or across the crevassed Sphinx Glacier, so a glacier is on the normal way in.
Guides call the Teepe Glacier and two cols the common approach to a snow and ice couloir, but none mentions crevasses on it, so the hazard is unconfirmed.
The approach traverses above a lingering snow patch in a couloir with no glacier, and an axe is only noted for early season.
It is a snow slope and ice chute whose descent is the Teepe Glacier, and nothing I read settles whether the route's own line is crevassed.
It is a boulder face near the toe of the Teepe Glacier, not on the ice, but the approach sits in an avalanche track and snow cover is unclear.
Warrior 1 is a Wind River cirque rock peak without a glacier, and the approach climbs snowfields whose lingering is not stated.
Parties often start up the Teton Glacier or from Owen, and the route text says snow and ice coverage varies by year.
The traverse rings the Dinwoody Glacier peaks and the party used snow pickets, but no source says whether the line crosses the ice.
Most parties come via the Lower Saddle Black Dike, but the other common approach goes up the Teepe Glacier, and upper snow depends on the year.
A rock face in a cirque without a glacier, where the walk-off couloir holds steep snow only early in the season.
A snow-filled northeast couloir with an ice smear lies right by the Teepe Glacier, and I could not confirm whether the approach crosses it.
The approach uses a trail toward the Teepe Glacier and then boulder hopping to the tower foot, never onto the ice, but snow cover is not stated.
A big-wall rock route on the west face of Fremont Peak where the only snow is a patch skirted at a belay.
The rack calls for an axe and crampons on Gannett, which carries glaciers, and nothing settles whether the traverse crosses them.
